_README: EVERY user-facing string in the product lives in this file. If you are adding text a person will read, add a key here and reference it — do not write it into a component. This file is also the answer to 'where does that word come from?', which is otherwise hard: strings assembled by code are invisible to search. TRAPS THAT HAVE ACTUALLY BITTEN, each more than once: (1) getTranslations() without a locale renders English inside an otherwise translated page — always pass { locale: params.locale, namespace }, adding params to the page signature if absent; not-found.tsx is the sole exception, since Next passes it no params, so it reads getLocale(). (2) Module-level constants (STEPS, TYPES, STATUS_STYLES, TABS) are evaluated at import where no translator exists — store labelKey and resolve at render. (3) Module-level FUNCTIONS have the same problem and cannot use hooks either; pass the translator in as an argument (see timeAgo in NotificationCenter). (4) Helpers that return finished English prose cannot be translated by their caller — return a key plus its values instead (see getDepositCopy and AllowanceReason). (5) A map or callback parameter named `t` silently shadows the translator. (6) Raw Prisma enums rendered with .toLowerCase() or .replace(/_/g,' ') stay English — use getEnumLabeller and add the values under `enum`. (7) Dates: toLocaleDateString('en-RW') pins dates to English; use lib/dates.ts, which carries real month names for all four locales. Also watch for ternaries, pluralising conditionals, and title-case text rendered uppercase by CSS — grepping the visible text finds none of them. Locale files other than en.json may be partial; missing keys fall back to English per key, which is why English must stay complete.
